{{Short description|German mathematician (1899–1971)}}
[[File:Krull,Wolfgang 1920 Göttingen.jpg|thumb|upright|Wolfgang Krull, Göttingen 1920]]
'''Wolfgang Krull''' (26 August 1899 – 12 April 1971) was a German [[mathematician]] who made fundamental contributions to [[commutative algebra]], introducing concepts that are now central to the subject.

Krull was born and went to school in [[Baden-Baden]].  He attended the Universities of [[University of Freiburg|Freiburg]], [[University of Rostock|Rostock]] and finally [[University of Göttingen|Göttingen]] from 1919–1921,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wolfgang Krull - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Krull/ |access-date=2022-10-12 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> where he earned his doctorate under [[Alfred Loewy]]. He worked as an instructor and professor at Freiburg, then spent a decade at the [[University of Erlangen]]. In 1939, Krull moved to become chair at the [[University of Bonn]], where he remained for the rest of his life. Wolfgang Krull was a member of the [[Nazi Party]].<ref>Florian Schmaltz: ''Kampfstoff-Forschung im Nationalsozialismus - Zur Kooperation von Kaiser-Wilhelm-Instituten, Militär und Industrie''. Wallstein Verlag, Göttingen 2005, {{ISBN|9783892448808}}, p. 333.</ref>

His 35 doctoral students include [[Wilfried Brauer]], [[Karl-Otto Stöhr]] and [[Jürgen Neukirch]].
